ربّ المشارق: ﴿وَرَبُّ ٱلْمَشَارِقِ﴾ — i.e., the points of the rising of the sun, and they are three hundred and sixty points of rising. Likewise the setting points, for the sun rises each day of the year at one of them and sets at one of the setting points. He dispensed with mentioning the setting points by mentioning the rising points, because they are equivalent to them, so they are understood from its mention.

With adornment of the stars. Nafi' and others read "adornment" as an annexed construct, with the stars following it. The word zīna (adornment) may be a verbal noun (maṣdar) or a noun for that with which something is adorned. If it is a verbal noun, then it is annexed to the agent, its sense being: "by the adorning of the stars" (zīnat al-kawākib, as a noun); or it is annexed to the object, its sense being: "by the adorning of the stars" (zayyana al-kawākib, the stars being the object). If it is a noun, then the annexation is explanatory (bayān) of the adornment. Ḥafṣ and Ḥamzah read zīnatin with tanwīn and khafḍ of al-kawākib, as an apposition (badal). They also read al-kawākib in the accusative, as the object of zīnatin, or as an apposition on the place (badal min mawḍi') of zīnatin.

﴿وَحِفْظاً﴾ is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), with the implied sense "and We guarded it with a guarding" (*wa-ḥafiẓnāhā ḥifẓan*). Alternatively, it is an object of purpose (*mafʿūl min ajlihi*), meaning "and for protection." The waw is either extra (*zāʾidah*), or the word is taken as governed by the sense of the sentence, because the meaning is: "We made the stars an adornment for the heaven and a protection." ﴿مَّارِدٍ﴾ means "extremely evil" (*ay shadīd al-sharr*).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 37, verse 8–10:

﴿They cannot listen to the exalted assembly﴾. The pronoun in "yasamma'un" (they listen) refers to the devils (shayatin), and "al-mala' al-a'la" (the exalted assembly) are the angels who dwell in the heavens. The meaning is that the devils are prevented from hearing the speech of the angels. Hafs, 'Asim and Hamza read "yassamma'un" with the sin and the mim doubled, its pattern being "yatafa''alun", and al-sam' (hearing) here means seeking to hear. Thus, on the first reading, hearing itself is negated, and on the reading with doubling, the seeking of hearing is negated. The first is more preponderant because of His saying: ﴿Indeed, they are removed from the hearing﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 212], and because the apparent sense of the reports is that they do listen, but they do not hear anything since the time Muhammad (ﷺ) was sent, because they are pelted with the stars. ﴿And they are pelted﴾, i.e., they are stoned, meaning with the stars, and these are the ones that people see shooting. Al-Naqqash and Makki said: the stars that pelt the devils are not the stars that move through the sky, because those do not have their movement seen, whereas these pelting stars have their movement seen because of their nearness to us. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "In this there is room for examination." ﴿Repelled﴾, i.e., driven away, distanced and humiliated, because "al-dahr" is pushing with violence. Its grammatical analysis: it is a object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlihi) or a verbal noun (masdar) of "yuqdhafun" in meaning, or a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial state (hal), its estimated form being: "madhhurin" (repelled). ﴿A perpetual punishment﴾, i.e., lasting, because they are pelted with the stars in this world, and then they are cast into Hell. ﴿Except one who snatches a snatch﴾: "man" is in the nominative position, a substitute (badal) for the pronoun in His saying: ﴿they cannot listen﴾, and the meaning is that the devils do not hear the news of the heavens except the devil who snatches a snatch. ﴿A piercing flame﴾, i.e., of intense brightness.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 37, verse 11:

﴿So ask them: are they stronger in creation, or those whom We have created?﴾ The pronoun refers to the disbelievers of Quraysh. Istiftā' (seeking a ruling or opinion) is a kind of questioning, as if it were a question directed at one whose words are taken into account and made a proof, since their answer to the question is something by which the proof is established against them. ﴿Those whom We have created﴾ is meant to include what was mentioned earlier: the angels, the heavens, the earth, the easts, and the stars. It was said that it refers to the earlier nations, but the first view is more preferred, due to the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, "am man 'addadnā" (or those whom We have counted). The purpose of the verse is to establish the proof against them in their denial of resurrection in the Hereafter, as if He is saying: these creations are stronger in creation than you, so just as We were able to create them, so too We are able to restore you after your passing away. ﴿Indeed, We created them from sticky clay﴾. Lāzib (sticky) means that which adheres and clings to what is adjacent to it, and describing them with this is meant to indicate the weakness of the creation of the children of Adam.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 37, verse 12:

﴿Nay, you wonder, and they mock﴾. That is, you wonder, O Muhammad, at their misguidance and their turning away from the truth; or you wonder at God's power over these great created beings mentioned. Ḥamza and al-Kisa'i read ʿajibtu with a damma on the tā' (ʿajibtu), and this presented a difficulty for those who say that wonder (taʿajjub) is impossible for God, so they interpreted it to mean that He made Him in a state at which people wonder. It was also said: its implied meaning is, "Say, O Muhammad, I wonder," and wonder has come from God in the Qur'an and the Hadith, such as his (ﷺ) saying: "Your Lord wonders at a young man who has no youthful folly (ṣabwa)." It is an attribute of action (ṣifat fiʿl). They considered it impossible for God only because they said that wonder is the magnification of a cause that is hidden, whereas the correct view is that it does not necessarily require a hidden cause, but is merely magnification; on this basis it is not impossible for God. ﴿And they mock﴾: the implied meaning is, "and they mock you, or mock the resurrection."

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 37, verse 14:

﴿وَإِذَا رَأَوْاْ آيَةً يَسْتَسْخِرُونَ﴾ ("And when they see a sign, they mock.") The sign here is the splitting of the moon (inshiqaq al-qamar) and the like. It is narrated that it was revealed concerning a polytheist named Rukana, to whom the Prophet ﷺ showed signs, but he did not believe. The word ﴿يَسْتَسْخِرُونَ﴾ (yastaskhirun) means "they mock," so the form (istaf'ala) is used with the same meaning as the basic verb (fa'ala). It was also said that its meaning is that some of them urge one another to mock, and it was said that they exaggerate in mockery.

"Will we, when we have died and become dust, [be raised]?" The verse means their disbelief in resurrection, and the discussion of the two interrogatives has already been given in (surah) al-Ra'd. "And our forefathers?" With the waw vowelled with a fatha, the interrogative hamza of denial has entered upon the conjunctive waw; it is also recited with the waw sukun, as a conjunction with "aw" (or).

Verse 28: ﴿They will say: "Indeed you used to come to us from the right."﴾ The pronoun in ﴿قَالُوا﴾ refers either to the weak among the disbelievers, who address their leaders among them in Hell, or to mankind, who address the jinn. Here "the right" (al-yamin) may carry three meanings. The first is that it means the path of goodness and righteousness; the expression for this uses the word "right," just as the expression for evil uses "left." The meaning is that they said to them: "You used to come to us by way of goodness, and so you would turn us away from it." The second is that it means strength, and the meaning on this reading is: "You used to come to us with your power and authority, commanding us to disbelieve and preventing us from faith." The third is that it means the oath (al-yamin) by which one swears, i.e., "You used to come to us swearing to us that you were upon the truth, so we would believe you in that and follow you."

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 37, verse 45:

﴿They are circulated among with a cup from a flowing spring﴾. Those who circulate among them are the youths (al-wildan), as stated in the other verse. ﴿bi-laadhhatin﴾ That is, "possessing delight," so it was described with the verbal noun (maṣdar) as a figure of expansiveness (ittisāʿan).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 37, verse 47:

﴿There is no harm (ghawl) in it﴾ Al-ghawl (ghawl): a general term for harm and injury. From it one says: "ghālahu yaghūluhu," meaning he destroyed him. It is said that al-ghawl is a pain in the stomach, and it is said that it is a headache. The prepositional phrase has been placed first here as an allusion to the wine of this world, because in it is the ghawl. ﴿Nor will they be intoxicated by it﴾, i.e., they will not become drunk from the wine of Paradise. Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 37, verses 88–89:

﴿So he cast a glance at the stars, and said: "Indeed I am sick."﴾ It is related that his people had a festival to which they would go out, and they invited him to go out with them. At that point he said, "Indeed I am sick," so that he would refrain from going out with them, and thus he could break their idols when they had gone out for their festival. As for the interpretation of this, there are three opinions. The first is that he was seized by a fever at a fixed time, so he looked at the stars to see the time of the fever, and he excused himself from going out because he was sick with fever. The second is that his people were astrologers, and he knew the rules of the stars, so he gave them the impression that he had reached, by looking into the science of the stars, the conclusion that he would fall sick, and so he excused himself from going out with them by citing the sickness he feared. The third is that the meaning of "he looked at the stars" is that he looked and reflected on what would happen to him with them, and said, "Indeed I am sick," and "the stars," according to this view, refers to what would befall his situation with them, and not the stars of the sky. This is far-fetched. His saying "Indeed I am sick," according to these opinions, may be understood as entirely true, with no falsehood in it and no figurative speech at all. But this is contradicted by what has been reported from the Prophet (ﷺ), that Abraham told three lies, the first of which was his saying "Indeed I am sick." It may also be that it was an outright lie, and he was permitted to do so because of this possibility, since he did it for the sake of God, intending to break the idols. It may also be that it belongs to the figurative (ma'arid) statements: if he meant that he would be sick in the future, since every person must fall ill, or he meant that he was sick in soul because of their disbelief and their denial of him. These two interpretations are preferable, because a blanket negation of lying contradicts the hadith, and an outright lie is not permissible for the prophets according to the scholars of verification (ahl al-tahqiq), whereas figurative speech (ma'arid, indirect expression) is permissible.

Ibn Juzayy, al-Tashil, on surah 37, verses 95–96:

﴿He said: Do you worship what you carve?﴾ That is, what you hew (tanjurun). An-naht (carving) is woodworking, an indication of their making (idols) from stone and wood. ﴿And Allah created you and what you make.﴾ Some scholars held that "ma" (ما) is a verbal-source particle (masdariyyah), and the meaning is: Allah created you and your deeds. It was also said that it is a negation particle (nafiyah), and it was said that it is an interrogative particle (istifhamiyyah), but both of these views are invalid.

﷿ Quranic verse: "And he said, 'Indeed, I am going to my Lord; He will guide me.'"

It was said: he said this after his departure from the fire, and he meant that he was going to his Lord through death, because he thought the fire would burn him. "He will guide me," according to the first view, means to the goodness of religion and worldly life; according to the second view, to Paradise. The Sufis said: its meaning is, "Indeed I am going to my Lord with my heart," that is, turning toward God wholly, with my entire being, leaving aside all else.

Lord, grant me a righteous son. ﴿رَبِّ هَبْ لِي مِنَ ٱلصَّالِحِينَ﴾ That is, a son from among the righteous. ﴿فَبَشَّرْنَاهُ بِغُلاَمٍ حَلِيمٍ﴾ That is, We gave him the good news of a forbearing boy, i.e., one of intellect (ʿāqil). ﴿Do you call upon Ba'l﴾ Ba'l (lord, master) in linguistic usage means "lord" in the dialect of the people of Yemen. It was also said: Ba'l is the name of an idol that was called Ba'labak.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 37, verse 130:

﴿Peace be upon Āl Yāsīn.﴾ Here, on this reading, "Āl" means "the people of" Yāsīn, a name for Ilyās (Elias). It is also said that it refers to his father, and it is also said that it refers to our master Muhammad (ﷺ). It is read as "Ilyāsīn" with a kasra on the hamza and the lām connected and unvocalized. On this reading, it is the plural of Ilyās, or a relative adjective derived from Ilyās, with the yā' dropped from it as it was dropped from "a'jamīn." It is also said that each member of the family of Yāsīn was named Ilyās, and then they were collectively called so. It is also said that it is a dialectal variant of Ilyās.

And We caused a gourd plant to grow over him. ﴿وَأَنبَتْنَا عَلَيْهِ شَجَرَةً مِّن يَقْطِينٍ﴾ That is, We made it grow above him, to shade him and shield him from the heat of the sun. Al-yaqtin means the gourd (al-qara'). God singled it out for him because it combines the coolness of shade, softness to the touch, and broad leaves, and flies do not come near it; for the flesh of Yunus, when he came out of the sea, could not bear flies. It was also said that yaqtin is any plant without a stem, such as vegetables, gourds and melons, but the first view is more well known.

Ibn Juzayy, *al-Tashil*, on Surah 37, verses 149–158:

﴿So ask them: "Has your Lord daughters while they have sons?"﴾ Al-Zamakhshari said: This is connected to His saying ﴿So ask them﴾ at the beginning of the surah, even though the two are far apart. The object pronoun refers to the Quraysh and the rest of the disbelievers. The meaning is: ask them in a manner of confirmation and rebuke about what they claim, that the angels are daughters of Allah. They assigned females to Allah and males to themselves, and ﴿that is an unjust division﴾. Then He put them to the test regarding what they claimed, that the angels are female, and refuted them by His saying ﴿or were they witnesses?﴾. It may mean "witnessing" in the sense of testimony, or "presence," meaning they were not present for that and did not know it. Then He informed of their lie in their saying ﴿Allah has begotten﴾. Then He put them to the test regarding what they claimed, that Allah chose daughters for Himself. All of this is a refutation of them and a rebuke to them. ﴿Exalted is Allah far above what they say.﴾

﴿Has He chosen daughters over sons?﴾ The interrogative hamza of confirmation and rebuke (hamzat al-taqrir wa-l-tawbikh) entered upon the connecting alif (alif al-wasl, the alif that is elided when a word is preceded by another word), so the connecting alif was dropped. Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 37, verses 161–163:

﴿So indeed you and what you worship, * you cannot lead astray concerning Him any [of them], * except those destined to burn in the Blazing Fire.﴾ This is an address to the disbelievers. This is a narration of the words of the angels (peace be upon them). Its implied meaning is: "There is none of us, [no angel], but he has a known station." The qualified noun was omitted (*hadhf al-mawsuf*, the omission of the noun described by an adjective) because the sense is understood. The "known station" (*maqam ma'lum*) may refer to a place where they stand, since some of them are in the lowest heaven, some in the second, some in the heavens, and some wherever God wills. It may also refer to a rank in worship, nearness, and honor.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 37, verse 165:

﴿And indeed, we are they who stand in ranks﴾. That is, those who stand in worship in rows. For this reason the Muslims were commanded to straighten the rows in their prayer, so that they might follow the angels; and none of the people of the other religions pray in rows except the Muslims.

ﷻ "And indeed, we are the ones who glorify Him." It was said: its meaning is "those who say: Glory be to Allah." In this statement, which the angels uttered, there is a refutation of those who claimed that they are the daughters of Allah and His partners, because they acknowledged themselves to be servants and obedient to Allah and affirmed His transcendence. This statement also indicates that what is meant by the jinn before this is the angels. It was also said that all of this is from the speech of our master Muhammad (ﷺ) and the speech of the Muslims, but the first view is more well-known.

Translation:

﴿So turn away from them for a time﴾. That is, turn away from them. This is a truce (muwada'a) abrogated by the sword (naskh). The "time" (hin) here is intended to refer to the Day of Badr. It is also said: the arrival of their appointed terms (ajal). And it is said: the Day of Resurrection.

And turn away from them, [for] they will see. (This is) a promise from the Prophet ﷺ and a warning to them. "Will they then seek to hasten Our punishment?" — an allusion to their saying: "When is this promise, if you are truthful?" and: "Then rain down upon us stones from the sky" [al-Anfal: 32] and the like.

"And when it descends upon their courtyard" — al-sahah (the courtyard): the open space around the house. The Arabs use this word for whatever befalls a person of harm and evil. "Evil is the morning of those who were warned" — al-sabah (morning) is used for the arrival of raids and calamities. The purpose of the verse is a threat of punishment that will descend upon them after they were warned, and the warning did not benefit them. This is an illustration: a sincere advisor warned them that an army would descend upon them, but they did not accept his advice, until the army came to them and destroyed them.

**﴿And see﴾** He repeats the command to turn away from them, along with the promise and the threat, for the sake of emphasis. It is also said: by the first threat he means the punishment of this world, and by the second the punishment of the Hereafter. If it is asked: why did He say earlier "abşirhum" (see them), and here say "abşir" (see), omitting the object pronoun? The answer has two aspects. The first is that mentioning it earlier sufficed him from mentioning it again, so he omitted it for brevity. The second is that he omitted it in order to convey generality, encompassing those already mentioned and others, as if He had said: "See all the disbelievers," unlike the first, which was specifically about the Quraysh.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 37, verses 180–182:

﴿Glory be to your Lord, the Lord of Might, above what they describe.﴾ He (Allah, exalted is He) declared Himself free of what the disbelievers attributed to Him that is unfitting for Him, for He related of them in this surah many abominable statements. As for "al-'izza" (might): if by it is meant the might of Allah, then the meaning of "Lord of Might" is "the One possessing might," and He added it to Himself because it is specific to Him. If by it is meant the might of the prophets and the believers, then the meaning of "Lord of Might" is its owner and its creator. From this, Muhammad ibn Sahnun said: whoever swears by the might of Allah, if he intends an attribute of Allah, then it is an oath; and if he intends the might which He bestowed upon His servants, then it is not an oath.

Then He concluded this surah with greeting upon the messengers: ﴿And praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds.﴾ As for the greeting upon the messengers, it may be that it means the salutation (tahiyya), or their safety from their enemies, and this would complete His saying: ﴿Indeed, they are the ones who will be given victory﴾ [al-Saffat: 172]. As for "al-hamd lillah" (praise be to Allah), it may mean praise to Allah for what is mentioned in this surah of the glorification of Allah, the support of the prophets, and other things; and it may mean praise to Allah in an unrestricted sense.
